parts: That door at the back of the cinema. You have walked past one a hundred times.
A heavy door, a sign above it, and a long bar across it.
You push the bar, and the door swings away from you. Almost every time.
That is not a coincidence. It is a design shaped by rules.
So why do emergency exit doors push outward?
Here is our reading, from simple mechanics. If a door opens inward, a crowd pushing toward it presses the door shut against its frame.
If it opens outward, that same push helps open it.
The sources we read do not spell out that physics, so it is our explanation, not a quote.
What they do tell is a story about rules. We will keep it calm, and stick to the design.
In eighteen eighty-three, in a theater in Sunderland, England, a door at the bottom of a staircase opened inward and was bolted. A disaster followed.
According to Wikipedia, public outrage and an inquiry led to legislation requiring entertainment venues to have a minimum number of outward-opening emergency exits.
Wikipedia says Robert Alexander Briggs, motivated by that disaster, received a United Kingdom patent in eighteen ninety-two for a panic bolt with a horizontal bar.
Wikipedia also links a theater fire in Chicago in nineteen oh three to changes. It says building and fire codes were reformed afterward, and exit doors had to be pushable from the inside.
We will not give one date or name for the rule. Wikipedia says adoption of such rules varies by place.
Now the bar. Wikipedia describes a crash bar as a spring-loaded bar fixed across a door that swings in the direction of an exit.
Press the bar, and it unlatches the door. It goes by many names: crash bar, panic bar, panic exit device.
Wikipedia says some exit latch designs were hard for people fleeing to open. Wikipedia adds that later patents describe a bar that makes a locked door pop open under simple pressure from inside.
Here is our reading. A bar can be pushed with a hand, a hip or a whole body, without having to think.
A knob asks you to grip and twist. A bar only asks you to push.

Here is a modern example. A Home Office guide for small and medium places of assembly in the United Kingdom, updated in twenty twenty-four, says exit doors on escape routes should normally open in the direction of travel.
The same guide says they should also be quickly and easily openable without the need for a key.
In the United States, Wikipedia says model building codes require crash bars in certain healthcare, education and assembly spaces. Adoption varies by city, county or state.
In Europe, Wikipedia says a standard, number eleven twenty-five, covers panic exit devices operated by a horizontal bar. We did not open the standards or the codes ourselves.
This video is not a guide to any building's rules. For that, ask the local fire authority.
Next time you enter a cinema, a theater or a hall, notice which way the exit doors swing.
Many swing in the direction you would walk to leave, often with a long bar. Not every door is built this way, and rules differ by place.
And it never hurts to notice where the exits are.
So the door that pushes outward is a piece of design shaped by rules.
Let us end on something lighter. Not every invention comes from a plan. Some come from an accident. Take the small yellow square on your monitor.
Its glue was meant to be very strong. Why does it barely stick?
